source_text: Χριστοῦ,» 3.16 πνεῦμα ἀληθείας, ὡς Ἰωάννης ἀπὸ τοῦ σωτῆρος εὐαγγελίζεται· «ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσατε· κἀγὼ ἐρωτήσω τὸν πατέρα, καὶ ἄλλον παράκλητον δώσει ὑμῖν, ἵνα ᾖ μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας,» καὶ πάλιν ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ αὐτοῦ ἐπιστολῇ. «καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν τὸ μαρτυροῦν, ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια,» ὁμοιότροπον τοῦ εἰπεῖν τὸν υἱόν· «ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀλήθεια.» 3.17 πνεῦμα θεῖον καὶ πνοὴ παντοκράτορος καὶ φιλάνθρωπον, κατὰ τὴν φράσιν Ἰὼβ καὶ τὴν πρὸ ὀλίγων στιχιδίων ἐν τῷ κεφαλαίῳ τούτῳ μνημονευθεῖσαν Μωυσέως. 3.18 ἀνευφημήθη καὶ φῶς τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑφ' ᾧ φωτιζόμεθα ὡς ἡνίκα ὁ ἀπόστολος γράφει· «ἵνα δῴη ὑμῖν πνεῦμα σοφίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως, ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ, πεφωτισμένους τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς καρδίας,» καὶ ὡς ∆αυὶδ ψάλλει· «ὅτι παρὰ σοὶ πηγὴ ζωῆς· ἐν τῷ φωτί σου ὀψόμεθα φῶς·» τουτέστιν ἐν τῷ υἱῷ σου, τῷ ἀπαυγάσματι τῆς δόξης σου τὸ ἅγιόν σου πνεῦμα. καί· «ἐσημειώθη ἐφ' ἡμᾶς τὸ φῶς τοῦ προσώπου σου, κύριε.» τί γὰρ ἂν εἴη ἄλλο τὸ πνεῦμα, ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἢ ἐκ τοῦ φωτὸς ἐκπορεύεται; περὶ οὗ Ἰωάννης ὕμνησεν ἐν μὲν τῇ πρώτῃ ἐπιστολῇ· «φῶς ὁ θεός,» ἐν δὲ εὐαγγελίῳ περὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς· «ἦν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινόν, ὃ φωτίζει πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐρχόμενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον,» καί· «ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς, ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωή.» 3.19 οὐδὲν δὲ θαυμαστόν, εἰ ἓν ὂν καὶ ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχον, διαφοροῖς προσηγορίαις δοξάζεται. τῷ γὰρ ἀπερίληπτον εἶναι θνητῶν λόγων τὴν ἄφραστον αὐτοῦ θεότητα, κατὰ δύναμιν τὰς εἰς ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς γινομένας ἐνεργείας ὑμνοῦντες, διαφοροῖς καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι προσχρώμεθα. 3.20 οἱ δὲ τὸ Μακεδονίου πρεσβεύοντες δόγμα, τῆς αἱρέσεως αὐτῶν μᾶλλον ἢ τἀληθοῦς γινόμενοι, οὐδέν τι συμβαῖνον τοῖς τῶν λογίων βλέπουσιν. συναρπακτικῶς γὰρ μυθεύονται ῥήμασιν αὐτοῖς, ὡς οὐ χρὴ ὁμωνυμίαις ἢ συνωνυμίαις ἢ ὁμοιολεξίαις προσέχειν. 3.21 τοῦ γὰρ θεοῦ, φησίν, τὸ «ἀγαθὸς» ὄνομα, τῷ «εἷς θεὸς» συμπέπλεκται ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι τῷ «ἀγαθὸς» ὀνόματι οὐ συνέζευκται τὸ «εἷς θεός». καὶ πάλιν· ἀγαθός, φησίν, ἐγράφη εἶναι καὶ ἄνθρωπος, ὡς ἡνίκα λέγει· «ἀγάθυνον, κύριε, τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς,» καί· «ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά.» 3.22 ὁμοίως δέ, φησίν, ἀγαθὰ ὁμωνύμως καὶ ἄψυχα, ὡς ὅταν προφητεύῃ· «ἐὰν θελήσητε καὶ ἀκούσητέ μου, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε.» ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ ἀνυποστάτων δῆθεν πραγμάτων εἴρηται· «ἀγαθὸν τὸ ἐξομολογεῖσθαι τῷ κυρίῳ.» 3.23 ὁμοίως ἅγιος, φησίν, καλεῖται καὶ ἄνθρωπος, δύναμίς τε θεοῦ, φησίν, καὶ σκώληξ, ᾗ γράφει· «ἡ κάμπη, ἡ δύναμίς μου, ἡ μεγάλη,» καὶ ὁ σωτὴρ δέ· «αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν σαλευθήσονται.» 3.24 καὶ τοῦτο μὲν φημὶ δὲ τὸ μὴ προσέχειν ὁμωνυμίαις καὶ ὁμοιολεξίαις λόγον ἔχει ἐπὶ τοῖς ἑτεροειδέσιν καὶ ἑτεροουσίοις, οὐ μέντοι ἐπὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος καὶ ἐκείνου, οὗ πνεῦμά ἐστιν, ἔτι μὴν καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ. προστιθεῖσα γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ τὴν ἀπὸ ἑαυτῆς ἀσφάλειαν ταῖς ὁμωνυμίαις ἢ συνωνυμίαις συμφράζει τὴν «μοῦ» ἢ «σοῦ» συλλαβὴν ἢ τὴν «ἅγιος» ἢ «ἀγαθὸς» λέξιν· τουτέστιν, ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ λέγει· «τὸ πνεῦμά μου,» ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ ∆αυὶδ καὶ ἡμῶν· «τὸ πνεῦμά σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν ὁδηγήσει με.» 3.25 πείθεσθαι οὖν δεῖ οἷς πολλῷ λυσιτελέστερον, ταῖς μνημονευθείσαις γραφικαῖς μαρτυρίαις λέγω, καὶ εἰδέναι ὡς τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν ἢ συνωνυμίαν καὶ τὰς ὁμοιολεξίας πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἔχει καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ αὐτοῦ υἱόν, τοὺς τοῖς ὁμοίοις ὀνόμασιν ὑμνηθέντας, οὐ πρὸς τὰ κτίσματα διὰ τὴν εὑρισκομένην ἔσθ' ὅτε ἐν ἐκείνοις ὁμωνυμίαν. 3.26 ταῦτα γὰρ εἰ καὶ δοίημεν ὀνόματί τινι ἢ λέξει θεῷ κοινωνεῖν, ἀλλ' οὐκ οὐσίᾳ οὐδὲ ἐνεργείᾳ δυνάμεως καὶ ἁγιασμοῦ. οὐδὲ γὰρ φύσει ταῦτα καθάπαξ ὑπάρχουσιν· κατὰ σύγκρισιν δὲ τοῦ κακοῦ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τοῦ ἁμαρτήματος ἤγουν τοῦ πάθους τὸ ἅγιον τέτακται· τὸ γὰρ μὴ λίαν κακὸν καὶ ἁμαρτωλόν ἤγουν ἐμπαθές ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἅγιον ἐνθάδε προσείρηται. 3.27 ὡς γὰρ κακία 48 καὶ ἁμαρτία ἤγουν πάθος καὶ ἀδυναμία ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι οὐχ εὑρίσκεται, ἅτε ἀγενήτῳ· οὕτως ἐν οὐδενὶ τῶν γενητῶν τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἅγιον καὶ δυνατὸν κατὰ τὸ τέλειον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ μετουσίαν· ὅπου δὲ οὐδαμοῦ ταῦτα κατὰ τὸ τέλειον, οὐδαμοῦ τὸ ἀγένητον. 3.28 ἔνθα γὰρ σκότος, οὐδαμοῦ τὸ φῶς· καὶ «ὅπου νύξ, οὐχ ἡμέρα. ὅθεν» εἴρηται καὶ τῷ Ἑρμῇ τῷ ἐπίκλην Τρισμεγίστῳ «ἀδύνατον ἐν γενέσει εἶναι τἀγαθόν, ἐν μόνῳ δὲ τῷ ἀγενήτῳ. ὥσπερ δὲ μετουσία πάντων ἐστὶν τῇ ὕλῃ δεδομένη, οὕτω καὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ.» 3.29 ὅμοιον τοίνυν καὶ ἴσον τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ
pass_a_gloss: [Ending the quotation from the previous section: the grace of our Lord Jesus] Christ'. 3.16 Spirit of truth, as John proclaims as good news from the Saviour: 'If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the Spirit of the truth may be with you for ever', and again in his first letter: 'and the Spirit is the one bearing witness, because the Spirit is the truth', in the same manner as the Son's saying: 'I am the truth'. 3.17 Divine spirit and breath of the Almighty and loving toward mankind, according to the phrase of Job and the phrase of Moses recalled a few short lines before in this chapter. 3.18 The Holy Spirit was also acclaimed as light, in whom and by whom we are enlightened, as when the apostle writes: 'that he may give you a spirit of wisdom and of revelation, in knowledge of him, the eyes of the heart having been enlightened', and as David sings: 'for with you is a spring of life; in your light we shall see light', that is, in your Son, the radiance of your glory, your Holy Spirit. And: 'the light of your face was marked as a sign upon us, Lord'. For what else could the Spirit be, which proceeds from the Father, or from the Light? About whom John sang in the first letter: 'God is light', and in the Gospel about the only-begotten: 'He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world', and: 'I am the light, I am the life'. 3.19 And nothing is astonishing if, being one and always holding in the same way, he is glorified by different titles. For because his unutterable Godhead is not to be encompassed by the words of mortals, singing according to our power of the workings that come about toward ourselves, we also make use of different names. 3.20 But those who champion the doctrine of Macedonius, becoming people of their heresy rather than of the truth, see nothing that agrees with the things of the oracles. For in a manner that snatches the hearer away they tell tales in so many words, that one ought not to attend to homonyms or synonyms or likenesses of wording. 3.21 For of God, he says, the name 'good' is woven together with 'one God'; but in the case of the Holy Spirit 'one God' is not yoked together with the name 'good'. And again: good, he says, man too was written to be, as when it says: 'Do good, Lord, to the good', and: 'the good man out of the good treasure casts out good things'. 3.22 And likewise, he says, lifeless things too are good by the same name, as when he prophesies: 'if you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land'. But also in the case of things, supposedly, without substance it has been said: 'It is good to give thanks to the Lord'. 3.23 Likewise, he says, a man too is called holy, and a grub too, he says, is called power of God, where it writes: 'the caterpillar, my power, the great one', and the Saviour too: 'the powers of the heavens will be shaken'. 3.24 And this, I say, the not attending to homonyms and likenesses of wording, has reason in the case of things of different form and different substance, but not in the case of the Holy Spirit and of that one whose Spirit he is, and further also of the Son. For Scripture, adding the safeguard from itself to the homonyms or synonyms, sets together with them the syllable 'my' or 'your' or the word 'holy' or 'good'; that is, either as from God it says: 'my Spirit', or as from David and us: 'your good Spirit will guide me'. 3.25 One must therefore be persuaded by what is much more profitable, I mean the scriptural testimonies recalled, and know that the Holy Spirit has the homonymy or synonymy and the likenesses of wording toward God and his only-begotten Son, who were hymned by the like names, not toward the creatures on account of the homonymy found sometimes in those. 3.26 For even if we were to grant that these share with God in some name or word, yet not in substance nor in working of power and sanctification. For neither do these belong by nature at all; but by comparison with the evil the good, and with sin, or rather passion, the holy has been ranked; for what is not very evil and sinful, or rather passionate, has here been called good and holy. 3.27 For as wickedness and sin, or rather passion and weakness, are not found in the one Holy Spirit, inasmuch as he is uncreated, so in none of the things that came to be are the good and holy and powerful according to perfection, but according to participation; and where these are nowhere according to perfection, nowhere is the uncreated. 3.28 For where there is darkness, nowhere is the light; and 'where night is, not day. Whence' it has been said also by Hermes surnamed Trismegistus: 'it is impossible for the good to be in coming into being, but in the uncreated alone. And just as a participation in all things is given to matter, so also in the good'. 3.29 Like, then, and equal is the Holy Spirit to the [Godhead, completed in the next section] of the Father and [the sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: He is the Spirit of truth, as John proclaims the good news from the Saviour: “If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the Spirit of truth may be with you for ever” (John 14:15-17). And again in his first letter: “And the Spirit is the one who bears witness, because the Spirit is the truth” (1 John 5:6). This is the same manner of speech as the Son’s saying, “I am the truth” (John 14:6).
He is divine Spirit, and the breath of the Almighty, and a lover of mankind, in the words of Job (Job 33:4) and in the words of Moses recalled a few lines above in this chapter (Exodus 31:3).

The Holy Spirit has also been hailed as light, in whom and by whom we are enlightened. So the apostle writes: “that he may give you a spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened” (Ephesians 1:17-18). And David sings: “For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9), that is, in your Son, the radiance of your glory (Hebrews 1:3), your Holy Spirit. And again: “The light of your face has been set as a sign upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:6). For what else could the Spirit be, who proceeds from the Father, that is, from the Light? Of the Father John sang in his first letter, “God is light” (1 John 1:5), and in the Gospel, of the Only-begotten: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9), and, “I am the light, I am the life” (John 8:12; John 11:25).

Nor is it any wonder if he, being one and remaining always the same, is glorified under different titles. For since his unspeakable Godhead cannot be grasped by the words of mortals, we sing, as far as we are able, of the workings that reach us, and so we make use of different names as well.

But those who champion the doctrine of Macedonius, belonging to their heresy rather than to the truth, see nothing that agrees with the words of Scripture. With words meant to carry the hearer off, they spin the tale, in so many words, that one need not pay attention to homonyms or synonyms or likenesses of wording.

“For with God,” they say, “the name ‘good’ is woven together with ‘one God’; but in the case of the Holy Spirit, ‘one God’ is not yoked to the name ‘good’.” And again: “Man too,” they say, “is written to be good, as when it says, ‘Do good, O Lord, to the good’ (Psalm 125:4), and, ‘The good man brings good things out of his good treasure’ (Matthew 12:35).”

“In the same way,” they say, “even lifeless things are called good by the same name, as when he prophesies, ‘If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land’ (Isaiah 1:19). It is said even of things that, of course, have no substance of their own: ‘It is good to give thanks to the Lord’ (Psalm 92:1).”

“Likewise,” they say, “a man too is called holy, and a grub too is called the power of God, where it is written, ‘The caterpillar, my great power’ (Joel 2:25); and the Saviour as well: ‘The powers of the heavens will be shaken’ (Matthew 24:29).”

Now this, I grant, not paying attention to homonyms and likenesses of wording, makes sense for things that differ in kind and in substance; but not for the Holy Spirit and him whose Spirit he is, nor, indeed, for the Son. For Scripture adds a safeguard of its own to the homonyms or synonyms, and sets beside them the syllable “my” or “your”, or the word “holy” or “good”. That is, it says either, as from God, “my Spirit”, or, as from David and from us, “Your good Spirit will lead me” (Psalm 143:10).

We must therefore be persuaded by what is far more profitable, I mean the scriptural testimonies already cited, and know that the Holy Spirit shares homonymy or synonymy and likenesses of wording with God and with his only-begotten Son, who are hymned under the same names, and not with the creatures, on account of the homonymy that is sometimes found in them.

For even if we were to grant that creatures share some name or word with God, they do not share his substance, nor the working of his power and sanctification. For these things do not belong to them by nature at all. Rather, “good” is ranked by comparison with evil, and “holy” by comparison with sin, or rather with passion. For what is not very evil and sinful, or given to passion, is here called good and holy.

For as wickedness and sin, that is, passion and weakness, are not found in the one Holy Spirit, since he is uncreated, so in none of the things that have come into being are the good, the holy and the powerful present in perfection, but only by participation. And where these are nowhere present in perfection, the uncreated is nowhere present.

For where there is darkness, there is no light at all; and “where there is night, there is no day.” Hence it was said even by Hermes, called Trismegistus: “It is impossible for the good to be in what comes into being; it is in the uncreated alone. And just as a share in all things has been given to matter, so too a share in the good.”

choices.issue: Garbled draft with a broken paragraph and wrong references
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English cut 3.22 in half ('Similarly, he says, good [is] the...' / 'Evenly and without soul'), so the claim that lifeless things are called good, and that a grub is called God's power (Joel 2:25), could not be read (reader report, Joel commentary SOURCE_ISSUES). It also rendered the command 'keep my commandments' as 'you have kept', 'we sing … we use' as 'they praise', the dative of agent 'by Hermes' as 'to Hermes', ἀνυπόστατα as 'unstable things', ἀγένητος as 'ungenerated', and 3.20 and 3.26 as nonsense ('nothing is happening to those looking at the logical arguments'; 'we should give a name or a word to participate in God'). Luke 6:45 corrected to Matthew 12:35 (the wording 'brings out of the good treasure' is Matthew's); 'I am the light, I am the life' given John 8:12 and John 11:25 instead of 11:25 alone; '(Matt 24:29)' written in full; Job 33:4, Exodus 31:3 and Hebrews 1:3 added. Fillers '[is]', '[the same nature]', '[designations]' removed.

choices.why: The section opens with the last word of the quotation begun at the end of the previous section ('the grace of our Lord Jesus'); only this word is translated.

The singular 'he says' introduces the Macedonian objector's argument in 3.21-3.23; rendered as the generic 'they say' so the reader does not take it for Scripture or Didymus. The objector's words are set in quotation marks.
Technical terms of logic: a name shared with a different sense, a name shared with the same sense, and similar wording; Didymus' argument depends on keeping them distinct.

choices.term: τί γὰρ ἂν εἴη ἄλλο τὸ πνεῦμα, ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἢ ἐκ τοῦ φωτὸς ἐκπορεύεται;
choices.english: For what else could the Spirit be, who proceeds from the Father, that is, from the Light?
choices.why: ἢ here equates the two names (the Father is the Light, as 1 John 1:5 then shows); 'what else' implies 'but light'.
The relative refers to the Father/Light just named; English names him so that 'God is light' is not read of the Spirit.

choices.english: uncreated / things that have come into being
choices.why: Single-nu ἀγένητος means not come into being (uncreated), not ἀγέννητος (unbegotten, the Father's property); the old 'ungenerated' blurred the two.

choices.english: even of things that, of course, have no substance of their own
choices.why: The objector's example is an action (giving thanks), which has no subsistence; δῆθεν marks it as obvious.

choices.term: σκώληξ … «ἡ κάμπη, ἡ δύναμίς μου, ἡ μεγάλη»
choices.english: a grub too is called the power of God … ‘The caterpillar, my great power’
choices.why: Joel 2:25 calls the locusts and caterpillar God's 'great power' (army); Didymus' objector cites it as a creature called 'power'.
The particles are awkward in the copy-text; Didymus concedes the objector's rule for creatures before limiting it.

choices.english: “where there is night, there is no day.” Hence
choices.why: The copy-text's closing quotation mark falls after ὅθεν; the quotation is closed after 'day', since 'Hence' introduces the Hermes saying.

choices.english: it was said even by Hermes
choices.why: Dative of agent with a perfect passive; Didymus cites the pagan Hermetic writings as a witness that the good belongs to the uncreated alone.
The section ends mid-phrase; the noun (Godhead) and 'of the Only-begotten' open the next section.
